name: Elderberry (Sambucus)
short: Case reports: autoimmune hepatitis on long-term supplements; grade 3 liver injury with pazopanib; possible pancreatitis. Linked to dermatomyositis flares at one clinic. Trial harms uncertain.
text: Case reports describe liver harm. A 2022 case report describes a patient who developed autoimmune hepatitis while taking elderberry-containing supplements long term, which the authors call a probable association; they note that there are no clear reports linking elderberry with autoimmune hepatitis or drug-induced hepatitis. A 2024 case report describes a middle-aged woman with soft-tissue sarcoma who had taken over-the-counter elderberry supplements for years and, by the fourth week of the cancer medicine pazopanib, had grade 3 liver injury (a fivefold rise in liver enzymes) with severe nausea and loose stools; all medicines, including the elderberry supplement, were stopped, and pazopanib was later restarted without the side effect coming back. The authors note that pazopanib is broken down by the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and that small laboratory studies found weak CYP3A4 inhibition by elderberry extracts, and they propose an interaction as a hypothesis; the abstract describes elderberry flower extract as the marketed supplement. A 2026 case report classes mild acute pancreatitis in a 75-year-old woman who took black elderberry extract daily, alongside long-term losartan, atenolol, niacin, aspirin and latanoprost, as possibly elderberry-associated; she improved with supportive care and stopping elderberry, and the authors could not rule out hidden biliary disease or the other medicines. In autoimmune skin disease, an observational study at one clinic that screened 673 adults with dermatomyositis or cutaneous lupus found that, among patients with dermatomyositis, 31% had disease onset or worsening after supplement treatment (10% of those with cutaneous lupus; the abstract does not say whether these shares are of all patients or of those taking supplements), and that elderberry was associated with the highest risk of worsening in both diseases (62% in dermatomyositis, 50% in cutaneous lupus); the abstract does not give how many took elderberry, and an association does not show cause. Allergy: in a 2003 study of patients with a history of summer hay fever tested in a routine setting, 0.6% of 3,668 randomly tested patients had a positive skin prick or blood (RAST) test to elderberry, and 9 patients with allergic symptoms due to elderberry were studied in detail; the authors write that allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and breathlessness may follow contact with the flowers or dietary products of the elder tree. A 1984 report is titled 'Poisoning from elderberry juice--California'; the record has no abstract, so it supports only its title. In a 2019 analysis of 42,344 accidental plant exposures reported to two German poison centres (in children aged 0.5 to 5 years, 98% were by mouth and 60% involved fruits), 26 plant genera accounted for 70% of all exposures, and elder (Sambucus species) was one of only eight of these that led to at least moderate symptoms; the abstract does not say which part of the plant was involved or how many exposures were to elder, and these data concern the plant, not supplements. On the other side, a 2021 systematic review of five randomized trials in viral respiratory illness found that, compared with oseltamivir, an elderberry-containing product may be associated with a lower risk of influenza complications and adverse events, found no evidence that elderberry overstimulates the immune system, and called the evidence on both benefits and harms uncertain. In a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in 52 healthy postmenopausal women, 26 of whom took an anthocyanin-rich elderberry extract by mouth and 26 placebo, liver and kidney function stayed within clinically acceptable ranges and markers including platelet reactivity did not change significantly; the abstract does not report adverse events. A 2014 review found no animal or human studies of the safety of elderberry in pregnancy, and concluded that health care personnel should not advise pregnant women to use it against respiratory infections. Interactions: the only interaction named in the cited sources is the proposed pazopanib interaction.
